title: Object-oriented programming
description: Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction and SOLID, with short Python and C++ snippets.

options: Bundling data with the methods that use it, and restricting direct access to the data
A class inheriting from several parents
Writing many functions with the same name
questions.explanation: Encapsulation keeps an object's state behind its methods (private fields, public methods), so the object controls how its data changes.

questions.prompt: Method overloading (same name, different parameter lists) is an example of:
questions.explanation: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types, before the program runs. Overriding a virtual method is resolved at runtime instead.

options: A class can extend several classes
A class can implement several interfaces but extend only one class
questions.explanation: Java allows single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation. Abstract classes can't be instantiated directly.

questions.prompt: "Objects of a subclass should be usable anywhere the base class is expected, without breaking the program." Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: The Liskov substitution principle, the L in SOLID. A classic violation is a Square subclass of Rectangle whose setWidth also changes the height.

questions.prompt: In C++, what makes a call through a base-class pointer run the derived class's version of a method?
options: Declaring the method `virtual` in the base class
questions.explanation: A `virtual` method is dispatched at runtime through the object's vtable. Without it, the call is bound at compile time to the pointer's static type.

questions.prompt: Which statement about constructors in C++ and Java is true?
options: They can only be called explicitly
A class can have only one
They have the same name as the class and no return type
questions.explanation: Constructors share the class name, declare no return type, run automatically when an object is created, and can be overloaded.

questions.prompt: A `Car` class holds an `Engine` object as a field. Which relationship is this?
questions.explanation: A car has an engine, so it's composition. Inheritance would claim a car is an engine. "Prefer composition over inheritance" is common design advice.

options: Hiding implementation details and exposing only what a user of the object needs
questions.explanation: Abstraction means showing the essential interface (e.g. `list.sort()`) and hiding how it works. Abstract classes and interfaces are one way to express it.

questions.prompt: In C++, you `delete` a derived object through a base-class pointer, and the base class destructor is **not** virtual. What happens?
options: Undefined behaviour; typically the derived destructor doesn't run
questions.explanation: Deleting through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour. In practice only the base destructor runs, so the derived part's resources leak. Give polymorphic base classes a virtual destructor.
